To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
partisans have become more hostile toward members of the opposing party and that this affective polarization has important consequences for the functioning of American politics.

affective polarization of American partisans has dramatically increased, that this polarization is based on social identity and affect for copartisans and oppositional affect for opposing partisans, and that this affect is ingrained and has consequences for nonpolitical judgments and behavior.
affective polarization of the American public is pervasive and consequential, and that this affect is based on party, not ideology.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the consequences of affective group polarization for American politics.
the consequences of a political system in which partisans are increasingly motivated to engage in hostile and discriminatory behaviors.
how affective polarization of the public has contributed to the breakdown of the political system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the American public has become more polarized over time not only because the parties have moved closer to the ideological poles, but also because partisan affect has intensified.
the polarization of affect toward opposing party members has become an important feature of American political life.
partisanship has become an important source of social identity and that the affect associated with this identity has become increasingly negative and polarized.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
affective polarization is real and consequential.
the polarization of the electorate is not just a matter of political attitudes and policy preferences but a broader social phenomenon.

the affective polarization of the American public has increased to a degree that has not been observed for other cleavages, such as race, gender, or religion, and that the consequences of this affective polarization are far-reaching and extend to the nonpolitical realm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
partisans’ negative affect for opposing partisans is not merely an incidental byproduct of the partisan divide; it is a key mechanism through which the divide is maintained and exacerbated.
the polarization of the U.S. electorate is not just a matter of partisans disagreeing on policy; it is a matter of partisanship itself being a source of disagreement.
the polarization of affect is not a mere byproduct of the political process, but rather is an important cause of political polarization.
